docs.title: What is appellate roulette?
docs.text:
The rule of law rests on a promise of generality: like cases will be treated alike, and the outcome of a legal dispute will turn on what the law requires rather than on the identity of the official who happens to apply it. This study subjects that promise to empirical scrutiny in federal criminal appeals.

  • Cases: the opinions of the twelve regional courts of appeals filed since January 1, 2010, from CourtListener, parsed and coded with courtpy.
  • Judges: who each judge of a panel is, who appointed the judge, and the judge's sex, race, age, and career, from the Federal Judicial Center's Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges.
  • Analysis: with amos, which records every step and parameter, so that the results can be reproduced.

docs.title: Research design
docs.text:
The study's methods are described in one settings file, studies/appellate_roulette.toml:

Unit One criminal appeal brought by the defendant and decided by a three-judge panel, all of whose judges are identified. Outcome outcome_criminal_defendant_won: whether the court reversed, vacated, or remanded. Treatment Which judges heard the appeal (panel_names), and the composition of the panel: how many of its judges were appointed by Democratic presidents, are women, are not white, were prosecutors or public defenders, are senior, or are visiting from another court, and their mean age. Comparison Appeals of the same circuit and year, among which the judges are drawn without regard to the merits.

It asks whether the outcome depends on the panel in three ways:

  1. The wheel (roulette, in roulette.py). How far the outcomes of each judge's appeals, and of each kind of panel, are from the outcomes of the other appeals of the same circuit and year is measured.
  2. The odds (fixest). A model of whether the defendant won, with a fixed effect for each circuit and each year, estimates how much one more judge of each kind on the panel changes the odds.
  3. Prediction (the analyst). Multiple models are trained to predict the outcome from the panel and the appeal, and tested on appeals that were held out. If the panel does not matter, shuffling its composition costs the best model nothing (permutation_importance).

docs.title: The opinions
docs.text:
CourtListener publishes its database as bulk files every three months. courtpy's own bulk download reads five of them, because CourtListener records the court of a case on its docket. This project's load_opinions (and the appellate-roulette opinions command) reads only the two that hold opinions:

File Size (2026-09-30) Read opinions 55 GB Yes: the text of each opinion. opinion-clusters 2.5 GB Yes: each decision's name, date, judges, and status. dockets 5.1 GB No. citations 0.1 GB No. courts under 1 MB No.

The file of opinions is nearly all of the download, and there is no smaller bulk file that holds the opinions of only some courts. What reading two files saves is mostly time: they are decompressed and read with every core of the computer (with indexed_bzip2 and pyarrow), which takes from half an hour to an hour rather than many hours. To download less, use the API (below).

Without the dockets, the court of each opinion is found from the opinion itself, by the rules in instructions/courts.csv: the website that CourtListener collected the opinion from (such as ca1.uscourts.gov), or else the court that the headmatter of its case names. Measured against the dockets, for the 375,994 decisions of the thirteen courts of appeals filed from 2010 through September 2026, the rules:

Find the court of 346,441 decisions (92.1%), and every decision filed since 2020 Put in the wrong court of appeals none Take for a court of appeals 4 opinions of other courts Find by year 83% of 2010, 85 to 89% of 2011 to 2017, 91% of 2018, 97.5% of 2019 Find by court 64% of the D.C. Circuit, 85% of the Fourth, 86% of the Seventh, 88% of the Federal, and 92 to 98% of the others

The decisions that are not found are the 29,423 that CourtListener has only from the Harvard Law School Library's scans of the printed reporters, which come with neither an address nor headmatter. About three fifths of them have the same name as (or a shorter form of the name of) a decision of the same court and day that is found, so they appear to be second copies. About a quarter (some 7,600, or 2% of all decisions) have no counterpart. Those are concentrated in 2010 and 2018, and a third of them are filed under the D.C. Circuit, where many are opinions of the district court that the dockets attribute to the court of appeals.

Two ways to add the decisions that are left out, both of which skip the cases that are already saved:

# With a CourtListener API key, which is stored in the system's keyring.
# About ten hours of requests at the API's pace, which can be stopped and
# resumed.
uv run appellate-roulette key set
uv run appellate-roulette download api --courts federal_circuits --start 2010-01-01 --folder data/court_listener

# Or from the bulk data with its dockets (5 GB more, and slower to read).
uv run appellate-roulette download bulk --courts federal_circuits --start 2010-01-01 --folder data/court_listener

Delete data/appeals.csv afterward, so that the added cases are parsed. To collect every case from the API instead, with no bulk files at all, set download = "api" in the settings (and remove parties, which only the bulk extraction uses).

CourtListener also holds some decisions more than once: an opinion that a court posted twice, or an opinion and an order in one appeal. About 3% of the decisions that name the United States repeat the court, day, and name of another. An appeal that is counted twice has the same judges and the same outcome both times, which would make the judges look as if they mattered, so the study keeps one decision for each court, day, and name (drop_duplicates).

docs.title: The variables
docs.text: Variable Meaning From outcome_criminal_defendant_won Whether the defendant won: the court reversed, vacated, or remanded in the defendant's appeal. courtpy's code_outcome type_criminal, appeal_by_defendant Whether the case is criminal, and whether the defendant brought the appeal. courtpy's code_case_type and code_parties panel_names, panel_found, panel_size The judges of the panel as the roster names them, how many were found, and how many the opinion names. courtpy's code_judges democratic_appointees, women, minority_judges, former_prosecutors, former_defenders, visiting_judges, senior_judges How many of the three judges are of each kind. The settings (derive_columns), from the roster's attributes panel_age The mean age of the judges. courtpy's code_judges criminal_*, civil_habeas, civil_aedpa The crimes and proceedings that the opinion discusses. courtpy's federal rules issue_* The issues of the appeal, such as suppression, sufficiency of the evidence, or the reasonableness of a sentence. studies/criminal_issues.csv

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
The study requires Python 3.11, 3.12, or 3.13 and uv. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

The first run downloads the two bulk files of opinions (about 58 GB, kept outside the project so that they can be used again) unless courtpy has already downloaded them, and the Federal Judicial Center's files of judges. No API key is needed.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
In the project's folder:

uv sync

courtpy is installed from GitHub until version 0.2.2 is on PyPI (see [tool.uv.sources] in pyproject.toml).

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Make the roster of judges once, and then run the study:

uv run appellate-roulette judges
uv run appellate-roulette run studies/appellate_roulette.toml --export

In Python:

import appellate_roulette

project = appellate_roulette.Project.create("studies/appellate_roulette.toml")
print(project.result.tables["balance"])
print(project.result.tables["roulette"])
print(project.result.tables["roulette_judges"].head(20))

appellate-roulette also runs any courtpy command (such as appellate-roulette rules studies/criminal_issues.csv) with this project's techniques available. To extract the opinions without running the study:

uv run appellate-roulette opinions --courts federal_circuits --parties "United States"

The first run saves:

File Holds data/court_listener/ One JSON file for each case, with its opinions. data/appeals.csv The coded cases. Later runs reuse it; delete it after changing the load_opinions_parameters section or the rules. results/ The tables, figures, and report of the analysis, with --export.

The tables to read first:

Table Holds balance For each thing that was true of an appeal before it was heard, the p-values of whether the judges and the composition of the panels predict it. roulette The test of the judges, the joint test of the composition, and a test of each attribute: the statistic, what chance alone would make it, and the p-value. roulette_judges For each judge, how many appeals the judge heard, how often the defendant won, how often the defendant won in the other appeals of the same circuits and years, and how unusual the difference is. fixest_coefficients The change in the log odds for one more judge of each kind. permutation_importance How much the best model's predictions worsen when each feature is shuffled.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Path Holds studies/ The settings of the study, and the rules for the issues of criminal appeals. src/appellate_roulette/opinions.py load_opinions and OpinionData, which extract the opinions. src/appellate_roulette/instructions/courts.csv The rules that find the court of an opinion. src/appellate_roulette/roulette.py roulette, balance, and spin, which test whether the draw of judges matters. tests/ Tests, with fictional judges and cases.

docs.title: How the court of an opinion is found
docs.text:
CourtListener records the court of a case on its docket, and this project does not read the dockets. OpinionData finds the court of each opinion with the rules in src/appellate_roulette/instructions/courts.csv, which are rules of courtpy and can be read, changed, and checked the same way:

uv run appellate-roulette rules src/appellate_roulette/instructions/courts.csv

The rules make one variable, court, from three pieces of text:

Target What it is What the rules do with it address Where CourtListener collected the opinion from (its download_url). The website of a court of appeals, or its package at govinfo.gov, gives the court. Any other address gives "other". opening The first 3,000 characters of the opinion, as plain text. A bankruptcy appellate panel named as the court at the top gives "other", since some panels post on the website of their circuit. Nothing else is taken from it. headmatter The start of the case as a printed reporter has it, for the decisions that CourtListener merged with the Harvard Law School Library's scans. "United States Court of Appeals, First Circuit" gives the court, unless another court, "certiorari", or "certified" comes first.

The first rule that matches wins, in the order of the file. An opinion that matches none is skipped, and a decision none of whose opinions match is left out. A decision whose court is "other" is left out as soon as that is known.

To use other rules, pass a file:

from appellate_roulette import OpinionData

data = OpinionData(rulebook="my_courts.csv")
data.extract("federal_circuits", "2010-01-01", folder="data/court_listener")

docs.title: How well the rules work
docs.text:
The rules were measured against the dockets of the bulk data of 2026-09-30, for every opinion of a decision filed since 2010 (3.3 million opinions, of which 394,881 are of the thirteen courts of appeals).

Decisions Of the courts of appeals, by the dockets 375,994 Found, in the right court 346,441 92.14% Found by the address 341,725 Found by the headmatter 4,716 Found, in the wrong court of appeals 0 Taken for a bankruptcy appellate panel 66 0.02% Not found 29,487 7.84%

The 66 are opinions of bankruptcy appellate panels that the dockets attribute to the Sixth and Eighth Circuits. Of the opinions of every other court, 4 were taken for a court of appeals, 2 of which are opinions of the Sixth Circuit that the dockets attribute to its bankruptcy appellate panel.

By how CourtListener got the decision (its source):

Source Found A court's website (C) 99.97% of 188,583 A court's website, merged with Harvard's scan (CU) 100% of 147,703 Harvard's scan only (U) 0% of 29,423 Other combinations 10,216 of 10,285

So the rule of thumb is simple: a decision that CourtListener collected from a court's website is found, and one that it has only from Harvard's scan is not. The courts' websites were collected from early 2010, and Harvard's scans end in 2018 or 2019, so the gap is in those years:

Year Found Year Found 2010 83.3% 2015 87.7% 2011 88.5% 2016 85.4% 2012 88.4% 2017 87.6% 2013 89.3% 2018 91.4% 2014 88.3% 2019 97.5%

Every later year is above 99.9%.

The decisions that are not found were compared with the decisions of the same court and day that are found, by the words of their names:

The Harvard-only decision Decisions Has the same name as one that is found 4,964 Has a name within (or around) the name of one that is found, as "United States v. Smith" is within "United States v. John Smith" 13,341 Shares a word of its name with one that is found 3,523 Has no counterpart 7,595

Most are second copies of decisions that are found. Of the 7,595 with no counterpart, 2,506 are attributed to the D.C. Circuit, and many of those are opinions of the district court. The rest are spread over the circuits, with the most in 2010 (before the courts' websites were collected) and in 2018.

docs.title: Adding the decisions that are left out
docs.text:
courtpy's own downloads save cases in the same form and the same folders, and skip the cases that are already saved. So either of them fills the gap:

# The API (a key is needed; about ten hours of requests for every circuit).
uv run appellate-roulette key set
uv run appellate-roulette download api --courts federal_circuits --start 2010-01-01 --end 2019-12-31 --folder data/court_listener

# The bulk data with its dockets.
uv run appellate-roulette download bulk --courts federal_circuits --start 2010-01-01 --end 2019-12-31 --folder data/court_listener

The API lists the cases of a court twenty at a time, and asks for the opinions of a page only if a case on it is missing, so the requests are few for the years in which nearly every case is saved. It waits when CourtListener asks it to slow down, and it can be stopped and run again, which resumes it.

Both add the second copies as well as the decisions with no counterpart. The study's drop_duplicates removes a copy only if its name is exactly the name of the other, so after filling the gap, compare the names of the appeals that share a court, a day, and a panel before relying on the results.

docs.title: The test
docs.text:
For the appeals of one stratum (a circuit in a year), let y be the outcome with the stratum's mean taken from it.

  • Judges. For judge j, d_j is the sum of y over the judge's appeals. If outcomes have nothing to do with judges, d_j has a mean of zero and a variance that follows from sampling the judge's appeals without replacement from each stratum. The statistic is the sum over judges of d_j squared divided by that variance. Judges with fewer than minimum appeals are left out of it.
  • An attribute. With x the attribute with its stratum's mean taken from it, the statistic is the slope of y on x.
  • Composition. The variation in y that all of the attributes explain together: the explained sum of squares of a regression of y on them.

Each is computed for the real outcomes and for each shuffle of the outcomes within strata. The p-value is the number of shuffles with a statistic at least as extreme as the real one, plus one, divided by the number of shuffles plus one, so it is never zero. For the judges and the composition, "extreme" means large. For an attribute, it means far from zero in either direction.

Shuffling outcomes within a stratum is the same as redrawing the panels among its appeals. It keeps the number of appeals that each judge heard, the panels that sat together, and the share of appeals that defendants won in each circuit and year.

docs.title: Changing the study
docs.text:
Everything about the study is in studies/appellate_roulette.toml:

To Change Study another period start_date and end_date of [load_opinions_parameters] Study every case, and not only those that name the United States Remove parties Study civil appeals The query of [filter_rows_parameters], the label of [general], and the covariates of [balance_parameters] Compare within finer strata strata of [balance_parameters] and [roulette_parameters], with any columns of the appeals Test other attributes of panels attributes of [roulette_parameters] (the default is every numeric column that starts with panel_) Add issues Rules in studies/criminal_issues.csv

Delete data/appeals.csv after changing the loader's parameters or the rules, so that the cases are parsed again.

docs.title: Added

The court of each opinion is found by the rules in instructions/courts.csv. The files are read with every core of the computer.

docs.title: Style Guidelines
docs.text:
This package follows the Google Python Style Guide with two notable exceptions:

  1. It always adds spaces around "=". This not only violates the Google guide, it violates PEP8, the foundational Python style guide from which all other resources are derived. I defy this strong, long-standing norm because I find it more readable. My brain and eyes have trouble seeing two separate objects when an equal sign is in the middle. I imagine that I am not alone in this accessibility issue. Further, as PEP8 itself notes, required spaces around equal signs are becoming increasing common with type annotations becoming part of best practices (and, as a result, signatures to classes, functions, and methods regularly include spaces around the equal signs). I realize that this will seem alien to many coders, but it is far easier on my eyes.
  2. I use some so-called "power features", primarily dunder methods, to make my interfaces easier to access and use. This is disfavored in the Google Python Style Guide because such code is often more difficult for others to read. To address that concern, I try to document and comment as to what the code is doing whenever I used any of the "power features" of Python.

Because of the first exception, the project does not use a code formatter (such as ruff format), which would remove those spaces.

docs.title: Test another outcome

roulette tests the study's label unless it is given another column:

strata = ["court_num", "year"]

Whether a panel publishes its opinion is the panel's choice, so this asks whether the draw of judges changes how often opinions are published.

docs.title: Test the judges of one circuit
docs.text:
import pandas as pd

from appellate_roulette import spin

appeals = pd.read_csv("data/appeals.csv", index_col="case_id", low_memory=False)
chosen = appeals[
    (appeals["court"] == "ca5")
    & (appeals["type_criminal"] == True)  # noqa: E712
    & (appeals["appeal_by_defendant"] == True)  # noqa: E712
    & (appeals["panel_size"] == 3)
    & (appeals["panel_found"] == 3)]
chosen = chosen.drop_duplicates(["court", "date_filed", "case_name"])
result = spin(
    chosen, "outcome_criminal_defendant_won", strata=["year"],
    attributes=["panel_party", "panel_woman"], simulations=5000, seed=43)
print(result.tests)
print(result.judges.head(10))

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This walks through the study from an empty folder to its results. Every command is run in the project's folder.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text: uv sync

docs.title: 2. Make the roster of judges
docs.text:
courtpy identifies the judges of each panel with a roster that it builds from the Federal Judicial Center's files. Make it once:

uv run appellate-roulette judges

The command prints where the roster was saved (courtpy's data folder, outside the project). Run it with --update to download the files again, which adds judges who have joined the bench since.

docs.title: 3. Try the extraction on a few cases
docs.text:
The opinions come from two of CourtListener's bulk files, which are about 58 GB together. They are downloaded the first time they are needed and kept in courtpy's data folder, so every later run (of this project, or of anything else that uses courtpy) reads the same copies.

To see what the extraction saves before committing to all of it, stop it after a thousand cases:

uv run appellate-roulette opinions --courts federal_circuits --parties "United States" --max-cases 1000 --folder data/sample

Each case is one JSON file, in a folder named for its court:

data/sample/ca4/167431.json
data/sample/ca5/78912.json
...

A case holds the decision (its name, date, judges, and status), its opinions, and nothing else. It has no docket and no citations, because the files that hold them are not read.

docs.title: 4. Run the study
docs.text:
uv run appellate-roulette run studies/appellate_roulette.toml --export

The first run:

  1. Extracts the cases of the twelve regional circuits that name the United States, filed since 2010, into data/court_listener (half an hour to an hour, once the bulk files are downloaded).
  2. Parses each case with courtpy's federal rules and the rules in studies/criminal_issues.csv, finds its parties, whether it is criminal, who appealed, and who won, and identifies its judges. The coded cases are saved in data/appeals.csv.
  3. Keeps the criminal appeals by defendants that three identified judges decided, once each.
  4. Tests whether the draw of judges is unrelated to the appeals (balance), and whether it changes their outcomes (roulette).
  5. Fits the logit model, trains and tests the three predictive models, and draws the figures.
  6. Saves everything in results.

Later runs start at step 3, because they reuse data/appeals.csv.

docs.title: 5. Read the results
docs.text:
Start with results/tables/balance.csv. Each row is something that was true of an appeal before any judge heard it, and each column is a p-value: whether the judges (judges_p), the composition of the panels taken together (composition_p), or one attribute of the panels predicts it. Under a random draw, these are spread evenly between 0 and 1. A table full of small values means that the draw was not random with respect to the appeals, and that roulette cannot be read as the effect of the judges.

Then read results/tables/roulette.csv:

Column Meaning statistic For judges, the sum over the judges of the squared difference between the outcomes of a judge's appeals and those of the other appeals of the same circuits and years, in standard deviations. For an attribute, the difference in the share of appeals that the defendant wins that goes with a difference of one in the attribute. For composition, how much of the variation in outcomes the attributes explain together. expected The mean of the statistic when the outcomes are shuffled. For judges it is about the number of judges tested. p_value The share of shuffles with a statistic at least as far from what chance makes as the real one. cases, units, simulations How many appeals, how many judges (or attributes), and how many shuffles.

results/tables/roulette_judges.csv has a row for each judge who heard enough appeals: how many, how often the defendant won (rate), how often the defendant won in the other appeals of the same circuits and years (expected), and how unusual the difference is (z and p_value). With a few hundred judges, a dozen with p-values under 0.05 are expected by chance, so the test of all the judges together is the one to rely on.

docs.text:
Whether the judges who happen to hear a federal criminal appeal change its outcome

The rule of law promises that like cases will be treated alike. This study tests that promise in federal criminal appeals. The courts of appeals assign judges to panels without regard to the cases, so if outcomes turned only on what the law requires, it would not matter which three judges heard an appeal.

The opinions come from CourtListener (see opinions), and are parsed and coded by courtpy, which also identifies the judges of each panel from the Federal Judicial Center's directory. The tests of whether the draw of judges matters are in roulette, and amos analyzes the result.

Importing appellate_roulette adds its techniques to the amos library, so that they can be named in a study's settings. It also sets pandas to keep text as Python does (the "mode.string_storage" option), which is what pandas does without pyarrow.

Contents

Balance: tests whether the judges who heard each case are related to what was true of the case before they heard it. LoadOpinions: collects, parses, and codes the opinions of the federal courts of appeals. OpinionData: extracts cases from the two bulk files of CourtListener that hold opinions. Project: amos.Project (which courtpy offers under the same name), which loads and analyzes the cases that a settings file describes. Roulette: tests whether the outcome of a case depends on the judges who heard it. spin: tests whether a column of the cases depends on their judges.

docs.text:
Bases: Describer

Tests whether the judges drawn are related to what a case was about.

Random assignment is what lets the outcomes of different panels be compared. It cannot be seen, but its consequences can: nothing that was true of a case before its judges were drawn (its "covariates", such as which side appealed or the crime charged) can depend on the draw. The table ("balance") has a row for each covariate, with the p-values of the tests that roulette applies to the outcome: "judges_p" (whether the covariate differs among judges) and "composition_p" (whether it goes with the composition of the panel), and the p-value of each attribute.

If assignment is random, the p-values are spread evenly between 0 and 1, so about one in twenty is below 0.05. Many small ones mean that cases of some kinds reach some judges more than others (as when a court sends some kinds of appeals to special panels), and that those kinds should be strata or be left out.

def describe(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    covariates: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    judges: str = 'panel_names',
    strata: Sequence[str] | str = ('court_num', 'year'),
    attributes: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    simulations: int = 1000,
    minimum: int = 20,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the tests of whether each covariate depends on the judges.

    Args:
        item: the dataset of cases.
        covariates: names of the columns that were true of each case
            before its judges were drawn. Defaults to `None`, which is an
            error: they must be named.
        judges: as for `Roulette.describe`.
        strata: as for `Roulette.describe`.
        attributes: as for `Roulette.describe`.
        simulations: number of times to shuffle each covariate. Defaults
            to 1,000.
        minimum: as for `Roulette.describe`.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if no covariates are named.

    Returns:
        The table, with a row for each covariate.

    """
    names = _listify(covariates)
    if not names:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} needs "covariates": the columns that were '
            f'true of each case before its judges were drawn'
        )
        raise ValueError(message)
    rows = {}
    for position, name in enumerate(names):
        result = spin(
            item.data, name, judges = judges, strata = _listify(strata),
            attributes = _attributes(item.data, attributes, name),
            simulations = int(simulations), minimum = int(minimum),
            seed = None if item.seed is None else item.seed + position)
        tests = result.tests
        row = {
            'cases': tests.loc['judges', 'cases'],
            'judges_p': tests.loc['judges', 'p_value'],
            'composition_p': tests.loc['composition', 'p_value']}
        for attribute in tests.index[2:]:
            row[f'{attribute}_p'] = tests.loc[attribute, 'p_value']
        rows[name] = row
    return pd.DataFrame.from_dict(rows, orient = 'index')

    start_date: str | None = None,

    max_cases: int | None = None,
    overwrite: bool = False,
    parties: str | None = None) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Saves the cases of `courts` filed between two dates.

    The opinion clusters file is read first, for the decisions filed
    between the dates. The opinions file is read next. The court of each
    opinion of those decisions is found (see `find_court`), and each case
    of `courts` is saved in a folder named for its court.

    Args:
        courts: CourtListener ids of federal courts of appeals (such as
            "ca1" or "cadc") or names of groups of them (such as
            "federal_circuits"). Defaults to "federal_appellate".
        start_date: earliest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None`
            (no earliest date).
        end_date: latest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None` (no
            latest date).
        folder: folder to save the cases in. Defaults to "court_listener".
        max_cases: most cases to save, for trying things out. Reading
            stops as soon as that many are found, so a case with several
            opinions may be saved without all of them. Defaults to `None`
            (every case).
        overwrite: whether to save cases that the folder already has.
            Defaults to `False`.

            United States as a party (as every federal criminal case
            does), or any other regular expression that the name of a
            case must match. Defaults to `None` (every case).

        ValueError: if one of `courts` is not a federal court of appeals.

    wanted = utilities.expand_courts(courts)
    unknown = [court for court in wanted if court not in COURTS]

        message = (
            f'{unknown} cannot be collected without the dockets, since '
            f'only the federal courts of appeals ({list(COURTS)}) can be '
            f'found from their opinions. Use `courtpy.BulkData` for '
            f'other courts.'

        raise ValueError(message)

    logger.info('extracting opinions from the bulk data of %s', date)

    skipped = set() if overwrite else _saved(folder)

def parts(
    self,
    kind: str,
    key: str,
    columns: Sequence[str]) -> Iterator[_Part]:
    """Yields the parts of a bulk file, with a way to get chosen rows.

    Most rows of a bulk file are not wanted, and making Python text of
    an opinion that is not wanted is most of the work of reading one. So
    each part of the file comes as one column to choose rows by, and a
    function that returns only the rows that are chosen.

    Args:
        kind: "opinion-clusters" or "opinions".
        key: name of the column to choose rows by.
        columns: names of the columns of the rows to return. Those that
            the file does not have are left out.

    Yields:
        For each part of the file, the values of `key` (as text, in the
            order of the rows), and a function that takes the places of
            rows in that part and returns each as a `dict` of `columns`,
            with an empty `str` for a missing value.

    """
    csv.field_size_limit(bulk._FIELD_LIMIT)
    with self._open(kind) as text:
        header = next(csv.reader(text, **bulk._DIALECT))
    kept = [name for name in columns if name in header]
    count = 0
    for values, rows in (
        self._parts_arrow(kind, key, kept) if pa is not None
        else self._parts_csv(kind, key, kept)):
        before, count = count, count + len(values)
        if before // bulk._REPORT_EVERY != count // bulk._REPORT_EVERY:
            logger.info('%s: %d rows read', kind, count)
        yield values, rows

def resolve_date(self) -> str:
    """Returns `date`, finding the newest files of opinions if needed.

    Raises:
        LookupError: if no date has both files of opinions.

    Returns:
        The date of the files to use, as YYYY-MM-DD.

    """
    if self.date is None:
        common: set[str] | None = None
        for kind in _KINDS:
            dates = set(self.available(kind))
            common = dates if common is None else common & dates
        if not common:
            message = 'no date in the bulk data has both files of opinions'
            raise LookupError(message)
        self.date = max(common)
    return self.date

def spin(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    outcome: str,
    *,
    judges: str = 'panel_names',
    strata: Sequence[str] = ('court_num', 'year'),
    attributes: Sequence[str] = (),
    simulations: int = 2000,
    minimum: int = 20,
    seed: int | None = None) -> Spin:
    """Tests whether a column of the cases depends on their judges.

    Cases with no value in `outcome` or in one of `strata` are left out. A
    case with no value of an attribute is left out of the tests of that
    attribute.

    Args:
        data: the cases, one row for each.
        outcome: name of the column to test: booleans or numbers.
        judges: name of the column that lists the judges who heard each case
            (as lists, or as text with "; " between names). Defaults to
            "panel_names".
        strata: names of the columns within which the judges are drawn at
            random. Defaults to "court_num" and "year".
        attributes: names of the columns of numbers or booleans that describe
            the composition of each panel. Defaults to an empty tuple.
        simulations: number of times to shuffle the outcomes within the
            strata. Defaults to 2,000.
        minimum: fewest cases that a judge must have heard to be tested.
            Defaults to 20.
        seed: seed for the shuffles, so that they can be repeated. Defaults
            to `None`.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `data` lacks a column that is named.
        ValueError: if there are no cases to test.

    Returns:
        The results (see `Spin`).

    """
    needed = [outcome, judges, *strata, *attributes]
    missing = [name for name in needed if name not in data.columns]
    if missing:
        message = f'the cases have no columns named {missing}'
        raise KeyError(message)
    values = _numbers(data[outcome])
    known = values.notna()
    for name in strata:
        known &= data[name].notna()
    cases = data.loc[known]
    if cases.empty:
        message = f'no case has a value of {outcome!r} and of {list(strata)}'
        raise ValueError(message)
    # The cases are put in the order of their strata, so that a shuffle
    # within the strata is a sort of each stratum's cases by random numbers.
    codes = cases.groupby(list(strata), sort = False).ngroup().to_numpy()
    order = np.argsort(codes, kind = 'stable')
    cases, codes = cases.iloc[order], codes[order]
    y = values.loc[known].to_numpy(dtype = float)[order]
    centered = _center(y, codes)
    names, incidence = _incidence(cases[judges])
    heard = np.asarray(incidence.sum(axis = 1)).ravel()
    spread = _spread(incidence, centered, codes)
    tested = (heard >= minimum) & (spread > 0)
    scale = np.sqrt(np.where(tested, spread, 1.0))
    columns = list(attributes)
    design = np.zeros((len(cases), len(columns)))
    for place, name in enumerate(columns):
        column = _numbers(cases[name]).to_numpy(dtype = float)
        present = ~np.isnan(column)
        design[present, place] = _center(column[present], codes[present])
    varied = np.asarray(design.any(axis = 0))
    sums = (design ** 2).sum(axis = 0)
    sums[~varied] = 1.0
    # The joint statistic is the part of the outcomes that the attributes
    # explain together, which the pseudo-inverse finds even when some
    # attributes are combinations of others.
    solver = np.linalg.pinv(design.T @ design) if columns else np.zeros((0, 0))

    def measure(outcomes: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, ...]:
        """Returns each statistic for each column of (shuffled) outcomes."""
        differences = (incidence @ outcomes) / scale[:, None]
        products = design.T @ outcomes
        return (
            differences,
            (differences[tested] ** 2).sum(axis = 0, keepdims = True),
            products / sums[:, None],
            (products * (solver @ products)).sum(axis = 0, keepdims = True))

    actual = measure(centered[:, None])
    shuffled = [
        measure(batch) for batch in _shuffles(
            centered, codes, simulations, np.random.default_rng(seed))]
    by_judge, dispersion, slopes, joint = (
        np.concatenate([batch[part] for batch in shuffled], axis = -1)
        for part in range(4))
    rows = {
        'judges': (
            actual[1][0, 0], dispersion.mean(),
            _p_value(actual[1], dispersion)[0], int(tested.sum()))}
    rows['composition'] = (
        actual[3][0, 0] if varied.any() else np.nan,
        joint.mean() if varied.any() else np.nan,
        _p_value(actual[3], joint)[0] if varied.any() else np.nan,
        int(varied.sum()))
    slope_p = _p_value(np.abs(actual[2]), np.abs(slopes))
    for place, name in enumerate(columns):
        rows[name] = (
            actual[2][place, 0] if varied[place] else np.nan,
            slopes[place].mean() if varied[place] else np.nan,
            slope_p[place] if varied[place] else np.nan, 1)
    tests = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(
        rows, orient = 'index',
        columns = ['statistic', 'expected', 'p_value', 'units'])
    if not centered.any():
        # Nothing can be learned from a column that is the same in every
        # case of each stratum.
        tests[['statistic', 'expected', 'p_value']] = np.nan
    tests.insert(3, 'cases', len(cases))
    tests['simulations'] = simulations
    totals = incidence @ y
    expected = incidence @ (y - centered)
    table = pd.DataFrame({
        'cases': heard.astype(int),
        'rate': totals / np.maximum(heard, 1),
        'expected': expected / np.maximum(heard, 1),
        'difference': (totals - expected) / np.maximum(heard, 1),
        'z': actual[0][:, 0],
        'p_value': _p_value(np.abs(actual[0]), np.abs(by_judge))},
        index = pd.Index(names, name = 'judge'))
    table = table.loc[tested].sort_values(
        'z', key = lambda column: -column.abs(), kind = 'stable')
    return Spin(tests = tests, judges = table)

Collects the opinions of the federal courts of appeals from CourtListener.

CourtListener publishes its whole database as bulk files every three months. courtpy's BulkData reads five of them, because CourtListener records the court of each case with its docket: the dockets file (about 5 GB, with a row for every case that CourtListener knows of, most of which have no opinion), the citations, and the courts, as well as the two files that hold the opinions. OpinionData reads only those two:

File Size (2026) Holds opinion-clusters about 2.5 GB Each decision's parties, judges, date, and status. opinions about 55 GB The text of each opinion.

Without the dockets, the court of each opinion is found from the opinion itself, by the rules in "instructions/courts.csv" (which can be read and changed in a spreadsheet, like courtpy's rules): the website that the opinion was collected from, or else the court that the headmatter of its case names. Only the federal courts of appeals can be found this way, because CourtListener collects their opinions from their own websites. An opinion whose court cannot be found is left out.

Measured against the dockets of the bulk data of 2026-09-30, for the decisions of the thirteen courts filed since 2010, the rules find 92.1% of the 375,994 decisions (and every one filed since 2020), put none in the wrong court, and take 4 opinions of other courts for a court of appeals. The decisions that they do not find are those that CourtListener has only from the Harvard Law School Library's scans of the reporters (8 to 17% of each year from 2010 to 2018), which come with neither an address nor headmatter. Most of them repeat a decision that was also collected from a court's website, and is found. The opening words of an opinion are not used to find its court, because they name the court below far more often than its own (as an order of the Supreme Court that denies certiorari does). The cases that are left out can be added to the same folder with courtpy, which skips the cases that are already there: from the API (courtpy download api, with a key) or from the bulk data with its dockets (courtpy download bulk).

Each case is saved in the form that courtpy's parser reads (see courtpy.courtlistener), with the decision, the opinions, and nothing else: no docket and no citations.

The files are read with pyarrow and decompressed with indexed_bzip2, which use every core of the computer, so reading them takes about half an hour rather than several. Without those packages, the files are read as courtpy reads them.

load_opinions is an amos loader, which is added to the amos library as soon as appellate_roulette is imported. It is courtpy's load_court_listener with one more way to download: "opinions".

    parties: str | None = None) -> list[pathlib.Path]:

    The opinion clusters file is read first, for the decisions filed
    between the dates. The opinions file is read next. The court of each
    opinion of those decisions is found (see `find_court`), and each case
    of `courts` is saved in a folder named for its court.

    Args:
        courts: CourtListener ids of federal courts of appeals (such as
            "ca1" or "cadc") or names of groups of them (such as
            "federal_circuits"). Defaults to "federal_appellate".
        start_date: earliest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None`
            (no earliest date).
        end_date: latest date filed, as YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to `None` (no
            latest date).
        folder: folder to save the cases in. Defaults to "court_listener".
        max_cases: most cases to save, for trying things out. Reading

            opinions may be saved without all of them. Defaults to `None`

            f'only the federal courts of appeals ({list(COURTS)}) can be '
            f'found from their opinions. Use `courtpy.BulkData` for '

def parts(
    self,
    kind: str,
    key: str,
    columns: Sequence[str]) -> Iterator[_Part]:
    """Yields the parts of a bulk file, with a way to get chosen rows.

    Most rows of a bulk file are not wanted, and making Python text of
    an opinion that is not wanted is most of the work of reading one. So
    each part of the file comes as one column to choose rows by, and a
    function that returns only the rows that are chosen.

    Args:
        kind: "opinion-clusters" or "opinions".
        key: name of the column to choose rows by.
        columns: names of the columns of the rows to return. Those that
            the file does not have are left out.

    Yields:
        For each part of the file, the values of `key` (as text, in the
            order of the rows), and a function that takes the places of
            rows in that part and returns each as a `dict` of `columns`,
            with an empty `str` for a missing value.

    """
    csv.field_size_limit(bulk._FIELD_LIMIT)
    with self._open(kind) as text:
        header = next(csv.reader(text, **bulk._DIALECT))
    kept = [name for name in columns if name in header]
    count = 0
    for values, rows in (
        self._parts_arrow(kind, key, kept) if pa is not None
        else self._parts_csv(kind, key, kept)):
        before, count = count, count + len(values)
        if before // bulk._REPORT_EVERY != count // bulk._REPORT_EVERY:
            logger.info('%s: %d rows read', kind, count)
        yield values, rows

def resolve_date(self) -> str:
    """Returns `date`, finding the newest files of opinions if needed.

    Raises:
        LookupError: if no date has both files of opinions.

    Returns:
        The date of the files to use, as YYYY-MM-DD.

    if self.date is None:
        common: set[str] | None = None
        for kind in _KINDS:
            dates = set(self.available(kind))
            common = dates if common is None else common & dates
        if not common:
            message = 'no date in the bulk data has both files of opinions'
            raise LookupError(message)
        self.date = max(common)
    return self.date

docs.title: roulette
docs.text:
Tests whether the judges who hear a case change its outcome.

The courts of appeals assign judges to panels, and cases to panels, without regard to the merits of the cases. So within one court in one year, which three judges hear an appeal is close to a draw from a wheel: appellate roulette. If outcomes turned only on what the law requires, the draw would not matter, and the appeals that any judge hears would come out like the other appeals of the same court and year, give or take chance.

spin measures how far the outcomes depart from that, and then finds out how large a departure chance alone would make by spinning the wheel again: it shuffles the outcomes among the cases of each court and year (each "stratum"), which breaks any tie between an outcome and the judges who reached it while keeping everything else as it was, and measures the departure again. The share of shuffles with a departure at least as large as the real one is the p-value. It makes no assumption about the distribution of outcomes, the number of cases that a judge hears, or how judges overlap on panels. It tests two things:

  • The judges. For each judge, the outcomes of the judge's cases are compared with the outcomes of all cases in the same strata. The statistic is the sum of the squared, standardized differences of every judge with enough cases, so it is large when who is on the panel matters, in either direction and for any reason.
  • The composition of the panel. For each attribute of a panel (such as the share of its judges appointed by Democratic presidents), the statistic is the difference in the outcome that goes with a difference of one in the attribute, among cases of the same stratum. A joint statistic asks whether the attributes together explain the outcomes.

Two techniques use it. Both are amos describers, which add tables to a dataset and leave its data unchanged, and both are added to the amos library as soon as appellate_roulette is imported:

  • roulette tests the outcome (the label of the study).
  • balance tests the draw itself, by asking the same questions of what was true of each case before any judge heard it (such as the crime charged). If the judges were drawn at random, the draw cannot predict those things, so small p-values here mean that the comparison is not a fair one.
Contents

Balance: tests whether the judges who heard each case are related to what was true of the case before they heard it. Roulette: tests whether the outcome of a case depends on the judges who heard it. Spin: the results of a test. spin: tests whether a column of the cases depends on their judges. _ATTRIBUTE_PREFIX: start of the names of the columns that describe the composition of a panel, which are tested unless others are named. _BATCH: number of shuffles that are made and measured at a time. _NOT_COMPOSITION: columns that start with _ATTRIBUTE_PREFIX but count the judges of a panel rather than describe them. _SEPARATOR: the text between names in a list that was saved as text. _attributes: returns the columns that describe the composition of each panel. _center: returns a column with the mean of its stratum taken from it. _incidence: returns which judges heard which cases. _listify: returns a setting as a list of names. _names: returns a cell of a table of cases as a list of names. _numbers: returns a column as numbers. _p_value: returns the share of shuffles at least as extreme as the data. _shuffles: yields the centered outcomes, shuffled within strata. _spread: returns how much chance alone would vary the outcomes of each judge.

docs.text:
Bases: Describer

Tests whether the judges drawn are related to what a case was about.

Random assignment is what lets the outcomes of different panels be compared. It cannot be seen, but its consequences can: nothing that was true of a case before its judges were drawn (its "covariates", such as which side appealed or the crime charged) can depend on the draw. The table ("balance") has a row for each covariate, with the p-values of the tests that roulette applies to the outcome: "judges_p" (whether the covariate differs among judges) and "composition_p" (whether it goes with the composition of the panel), and the p-value of each attribute.

If assignment is random, the p-values are spread evenly between 0 and 1, so about one in twenty is below 0.05. Many small ones mean that cases of some kinds reach some judges more than others (as when a court sends some kinds of appeals to special panels), and that those kinds should be strata or be left out.

def describe(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    covariates: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    judges: str = 'panel_names',
    strata: Sequence[str] | str = ('court_num', 'year'),
    attributes: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    simulations: int = 1000,
    minimum: int = 20,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the tests of whether each covariate depends on the judges.

    Args:
        item: the dataset of cases.
        covariates: names of the columns that were true of each case
            before its judges were drawn. Defaults to `None`, which is an
            error: they must be named.
        judges: as for `Roulette.describe`.
        strata: as for `Roulette.describe`.
        attributes: as for `Roulette.describe`.
        simulations: number of times to shuffle each covariate. Defaults
            to 1,000.
        minimum: as for `Roulette.describe`.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if no covariates are named.

    Returns:
        The table, with a row for each covariate.

    """
    names = _listify(covariates)
    if not names:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} needs "covariates": the columns that were '
            f'true of each case before its judges were drawn'
        )
        raise ValueError(message)
    rows = {}
    for position, name in enumerate(names):
        result = spin(
            item.data, name, judges = judges, strata = _listify(strata),
            attributes = _attributes(item.data, attributes, name),
            simulations = int(simulations), minimum = int(minimum),
            seed = None if item.seed is None else item.seed + position)
        tests = result.tests
        row = {
            'cases': tests.loc['judges', 'cases'],
            'judges_p': tests.loc['judges', 'p_value'],
            'composition_p': tests.loc['composition', 'p_value']}
        for attribute in tests.index[2:]:
            row[f'{attribute}_p'] = tests.loc[attribute, 'p_value']
        rows[name] = row
    return pd.DataFrame.from_dict(rows, orient = 'index')

Tests whether the outcome of a case depends on the judges who heard it.

The table that it adds ("roulette") has a row for each test (see Spin), and "roulette_judges" has a row for each judge. A small p-value in the "judges" row means that outcomes differ among judges by more than chance would make them, and one in the row of an attribute means that the outcome goes with that attribute of the panel.

With hundreds of judges, some have small p-values of their own by chance alone, so the table of judges shows where the differences are, and the "judges" row says whether there are any.

def spin(
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    outcome: str,
    *,
    judges: str = 'panel_names',
    strata: Sequence[str] = ('court_num', 'year'),
    attributes: Sequence[str] = (),
    simulations: int = 2000,
    minimum: int = 20,
    seed: int | None = None) -> Spin:
    """Tests whether a column of the cases depends on their judges.

    Cases with no value in `outcome` or in one of `strata` are left out. A
    case with no value of an attribute is left out of the tests of that
    attribute.

    Args:
        data: the cases, one row for each.
        outcome: name of the column to test: booleans or numbers.
        judges: name of the column that lists the judges who heard each case
            (as lists, or as text with "; " between names). Defaults to
            "panel_names".
        strata: names of the columns within which the judges are drawn at
            random. Defaults to "court_num" and "year".
        attributes: names of the columns of numbers or booleans that describe
            the composition of each panel. Defaults to an empty tuple.
        simulations: number of times to shuffle the outcomes within the
            strata. Defaults to 2,000.
        minimum: fewest cases that a judge must have heard to be tested.
            Defaults to 20.
        seed: seed for the shuffles, so that they can be repeated. Defaults
            to `None`.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `data` lacks a column that is named.
        ValueError: if there are no cases to test.

    Returns:
        The results (see `Spin`).

    """
    needed = [outcome, judges, *strata, *attributes]
    missing = [name for name in needed if name not in data.columns]
    if missing:
        message = f'the cases have no columns named {missing}'
        raise KeyError(message)
    values = _numbers(data[outcome])
    known = values.notna()
    for name in strata:
        known &= data[name].notna()
    cases = data.loc[known]
    if cases.empty:
        message = f'no case has a value of {outcome!r} and of {list(strata)}'
        raise ValueError(message)
    # The cases are put in the order of their strata, so that a shuffle
    # within the strata is a sort of each stratum's cases by random numbers.
    codes = cases.groupby(list(strata), sort = False).ngroup().to_numpy()
    order = np.argsort(codes, kind = 'stable')
    cases, codes = cases.iloc[order], codes[order]
    y = values.loc[known].to_numpy(dtype = float)[order]
    centered = _center(y, codes)
    names, incidence = _incidence(cases[judges])
    heard = np.asarray(incidence.sum(axis = 1)).ravel()
    spread = _spread(incidence, centered, codes)
    tested = (heard >= minimum) & (spread > 0)
    scale = np.sqrt(np.where(tested, spread, 1.0))
    columns = list(attributes)
    design = np.zeros((len(cases), len(columns)))
    for place, name in enumerate(columns):
        column = _numbers(cases[name]).to_numpy(dtype = float)
        present = ~np.isnan(column)
        design[present, place] = _center(column[present], codes[present])
    varied = np.asarray(design.any(axis = 0))
    sums = (design ** 2).sum(axis = 0)
    sums[~varied] = 1.0
    # The joint statistic is the part of the outcomes that the attributes
    # explain together, which the pseudo-inverse finds even when some
    # attributes are combinations of others.
    solver = np.linalg.pinv(design.T @ design) if columns else np.zeros((0, 0))

    def measure(outcomes: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, ...]:
        """Returns each statistic for each column of (shuffled) outcomes."""
        differences = (incidence @ outcomes) / scale[:, None]
        products = design.T @ outcomes
        return (
            differences,
            (differences[tested] ** 2).sum(axis = 0, keepdims = True),
            products / sums[:, None],
            (products * (solver @ products)).sum(axis = 0, keepdims = True))

    actual = measure(centered[:, None])
    shuffled = [
        measure(batch) for batch in _shuffles(
            centered, codes, simulations, np.random.default_rng(seed))]
    by_judge, dispersion, slopes, joint = (
        np.concatenate([batch[part] for batch in shuffled], axis = -1)
        for part in range(4))
    rows = {
        'judges': (
            actual[1][0, 0], dispersion.mean(),
            _p_value(actual[1], dispersion)[0], int(tested.sum()))}
    rows['composition'] = (
        actual[3][0, 0] if varied.any() else np.nan,
        joint.mean() if varied.any() else np.nan,
        _p_value(actual[3], joint)[0] if varied.any() else np.nan,
        int(varied.sum()))
    slope_p = _p_value(np.abs(actual[2]), np.abs(slopes))
    for place, name in enumerate(columns):
        rows[name] = (
            actual[2][place, 0] if varied[place] else np.nan,
            slopes[place].mean() if varied[place] else np.nan,
            slope_p[place] if varied[place] else np.nan, 1)
    tests = pd.DataFrame.from_dict(
        rows, orient = 'index',
        columns = ['statistic', 'expected', 'p_value', 'units'])
    if not centered.any():
        # Nothing can be learned from a column that is the same in every
        # case of each stratum.
        tests[['statistic', 'expected', 'p_value']] = np.nan
    tests.insert(3, 'cases', len(cases))
    tests['simulations'] = simulations
    totals = incidence @ y
    expected = incidence @ (y - centered)
    table = pd.DataFrame({
        'cases': heard.astype(int),
        'rate': totals / np.maximum(heard, 1),
        'expected': expected / np.maximum(heard, 1),
        'difference': (totals - expected) / np.maximum(heard, 1),
        'z': actual[0][:, 0],
        'p_value': _p_value(np.abs(actual[0]), np.abs(by_judge))},
        index = pd.Index(names, name = 'judge'))
    table = table.loc[tested].sort_values(
        'z', key = lambda column: -column.abs(), kind = 'stable')
    return Spin(tests = tests, judges = table)
